record.paper_title: Addition Machines, Automatic Functions and Open Problems of Floyd and Knuth
record.context_brief: five-register linear-time squaring and integer division
record.original_question: In Floyd and Knuth's integer addition-machine model, registers hold integers and the unit-cost primitive instructions include adding or subtracting register contents, comparing register contents with conditional branching, unconditional jumps, reading input, and writing output. Without treating arbitrary integer constants as primitive register operations, can an integer addition machine using only five registers compute the square x^2 of an integer input x in O(log x) operations, and can such a machine compute the integer quotient floor(y/z), for inputs where the quotient is defined, in O(log(y/z)) operations?

evidence.quote: The precise model of Floyd and Knuth [13] allows the following primitive operations which count each as 1 step: Adding or subtracting two registers
(2) Can an integer addition machine with only 5 registers compute x2 in O(log x) operations? Can it compute the quotient floor(y/z) in O(log y/z) operations?
In Open Problem (2) they asked whether the number of five registers to do squaring, integer multiplication and integer division in linear time can be obtained and the answer is affirmative.

artifact.status_search_result: Both questions have been resolved affirmatively. Work on addition machines and automatic functions shows that five registers suffice for squaring, integer multiplication, and integer division within the desired logarithmic-step bounds, even under the restriction that arbitrary integer constants are not allowed as primitives.

status_evidence.title: Addition Machines, Automatic Functions and Open Problems of Floyd and Knuth (arXiv:2111.08969)
status_evidence.snippet: Floyd and Knuth investigated in 1990 register machines... whether their current bound on the number of registers for multiplying and dividing fast can be improved... Both questions are answered positively.
status_evidence.claim: The five-register question for squaring and integer division in linear time is answered affirmatively.
